Protecting Every Route in a Resource

One router.use(authenticate) call, ahead of every route on that router — nested comment routes inherit it for free.

authenticate (previous slide) is only useful applied somewhere — and rather than adding it to every individual route one at a time, each resource router applies it once, at the top:

// Figure 4.8: authenticating an entire router at once (src/routes/ticket.routes.js, excerpt)
const router = express.Router();

// Applies to every route below, including the nested comment routes
// mounted at the bottom of this file.
router.use(authenticate);

router.get('/', validate({ query: listTicketsQuerySchema }), ticketController.getAllTickets);
// ...every other /tickets route...

router.use('/:ticketId/comments', commentRoutes);

router.use(authenticate), with no path, matches every request this router ever handles — Express runs middleware in the order it's registered, so by the time any router.get/router.post/etc. below it runs, req.user is already set. That includes router.use('/:ticketId/ comments', commentRoutes) at the bottom (Lesson 3's nested-routes topic): comment.routes.js never calls authenticate itself, and doesn't need to — a request to /tickets/1/comments already passed through ticket.routes.js's authenticate before Express ever hands it off to the nested router, the same way :ticketId itself reaches comment.routes.js via mergeParams.

auth.routes.js is the one router in this project that deliberately never calls authenticate — /auth/register and /auth/login are how a client gets a token in the first place, so requiring one to reach them would make getting one impossible.
